 Tax IRS finalizes rules for 401(k), 403(b) automatic enrollment 
 By Michael Cohn CloseText About Michael 
 twitter mikecohnat 
 mailto michael.cohn@arizent.com 
 linkedin micohn 
 Published November 17, 2026, 10:24 a.m. EST | Updated November 17, 2026, 11:53 a.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 stock.adobe.com Key Insight: See why federal regulators are shifting the rules for automatic 401(k) and 403(b) enrollments.
 Forward Look: Get ready for new automatic enrollment rules to take effect after Dec. 31, 2027.
 The Internal Revenue Service and the Treasury Department released final regulations implementing a provision of the SECURE 2.0 Act providing automatic enrollment in 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans.
 Processing Content The SECURE 2.0 Act, enacted in December 2022, included a large number of changes for retirement and tax planning, including an expansion of automatic enrollment in retirement plans. SECURE 2.0 requires 401(k) and 403(b) plans to automatically enroll participants in the respective plans upon becoming eligible, although employees can then opt out of coverage.  
 The final regulations posted Tuesday provide employers with guidance on the automatic enrollment rules for certain 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans, with the goal of helping workers build their retirement savings while preserving their control over how much they contribute. The final regulations clarify the requirements for plan sponsors and simplify certain participant notices. A 403(b) plan, which is also known as a tax-sheltered annuity plan, is a tax-advantaged workplace retirement account designed for employees of public schools, universities, hospitals, churches, and certain 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. It functions similarly to a private-sector 401(k), allowing employees to save and invest for retirement directly through payroll deductions.
 The Treasury estimates that SECURE 2.0's automatic enrollment expansion provision will increase retirement savings by an average of $4.2 billion annually over the 2023-2032 period.
 "With the SECURE 2.0 regulations in place, American families will be able to boost their savings and keep more of their hard-earned money through their automatic enrollment in a retirement account," said IRS CEO Frank Bisignano in a statement. "These regulations reduce the administrative burden placed on taxpayers when making long-term financial decisions. More broadly, they further the IRS goal of improving taxpayer service by making interactions with the Service simpler and easier."
 The covered retirement plans generally must automatically enroll eligible employees at a contribution rate of 3%. After an initial participation period, the default contribution rate must generally increase by at least one percentage point each year until it reaches at least ten percent, subject to a fifteen percent maximum. Employees can opt out or choose a different contribution rate. 
 The final regulations generally apply to retirement plan years starting after Dec. 31, 2027, giving employers time to make the necessary administrative changes. 
 "A financially secure retirement is a cornerstone of the American Dream, and every worker deserves the opportunity to achieve it," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "Today's rules help more American families and workers build retirement savings while keeping them in control of their contributions, and give employers the clarity and flexibility to invest in their employees' futures."
 The final regulations clarify the statutory exceptions for qualifying small and new businesses, governmental plans, church plans and SIMPLE 401(k) plans. They also give employers more flexibility in the timing and amount of automatic contribution increases, within statutory limits.
 The rules aim to simplify plan communications by permitting certain required notices to be combined and reducing annual notice requirements for qualifying employees who are not participating, provided they receive annual reminders and any plan documents they are entitled to request. They also explain how automatic enrollment requirements apply after plan mergers.
